notes.front: In aviation, what is an aircraft drawing?
notes.back: A method of conveying ideas about the construction or assembly of objects, using lines, notes, abbreviations and symbols.
notes.explanation: Drawings are used to avoid the errors that descriptions invite, which is why the handbook calls drawing the draftsman’s language.
notes.example: Like a written parts description, but a misplaced comma cannot change what the lines show.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Introduction”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: To avoid these possible errors, drawings are used to describe objects. For this reason, drawing is the draftsman’s language. Drawing, in the aviation industry, is a method of conveying ideas concerning the construction or assembly of objects. This is done with the help of lines, notes, abbreviations, and symbols.

notes.front: What is a detail drawing?
notes.back: A description of a single part, giving the specifications for its size, shape, material and methods of manufacture.
notes.explanation: Detail drawings are usually rather simple, and several may share one sheet when the parts are small.
notes.example: Like a recipe card for one bracket: its size, shape, the aluminium to use and how to make it, but nothing about what it bolts to.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Detail Drawing”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: A detail drawing is a description of a single part, describing bylines, notes, and symbols the specifications for size, shape, material, and methods of manufacture to be used in making the part.

notes.front: What is an assembly drawing?
notes.back: A description of an object made up of two or more parts, giving its size and shape.
notes.explanation: Its primary purpose is to show how the various parts relate to one another.
notes.example: Like a detail drawing, but for a hinge made of a leaf, a pin and a bushing, showing how the three fit together.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Assembly Drawing”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: An assembly drawing is a description of an object made up of two or more parts. [Figure 4-4] It describes the object’s size and shape. Its primary purpose is to show the relationship of the various parts.

notes.front: What is an installation drawing?
notes.back: A drawing that includes all necessary information for a part or assembly in its final installed position in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: It gives the dimensions that locate specific parts relative to other parts, plus reference dimensions helpful in later shop work.
notes.example: Like an assembly drawing, but it shows where a finished pump bracket sits in the wheel well relative to the surrounding structure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Installation Drawing”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: An installation drawing is one that includes all necessary information for a part or an assembly in the final installed position in the aircraft.

notes.front: What is a sectional view?
notes.back: A view obtained by cutting away part of an object to show its shape and construction at the cutting plane.
notes.explanation: The parts cut away are shown with section, or crosshatching, lines.
notes.example: Like slicing a sausage roll and drawing the cut face, so the filling inside shows.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Sectional View Drawings”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: A section or sectional view is obtained by cutting away part of an object to show the shape and construction at the cutting plane. The part or parts cut away are shown by using section (crosshatching) lines.

notes.front: What is a title block on a print?
notes.back: The block that identifies the print: a drawing number and other data about the drawing and the object it represents.
notes.explanation: Every print must have some means of identification, and the title block provides it.
notes.example: Like the label on a map’s corner that names the map, its scale, its date and who drew it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Title Blocks”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: Every print must have some means of identification. This is provided by a title block. [Figure 4-4A] The title block consists of a drawing number and certain other data concerning the drawing and the object it represents.

notes.front: What is a dash number on a drawing?
notes.back: An individual number added to the drawing number when a drawing shows more than one detail, as in 40267-1 and 40267-2.
notes.explanation: Both parts carry the same drawing number, and the dash number tells them apart.
notes.example: Like flat numbers in one building: the street number is shared and the number after it picks out each flat.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reference and Dash Numbers”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: When more than one detail is shown on a drawing, dash numbers are used. Both parts would have the same drawing number plus an individual number, such as 40267-1 and 40267-2.

notes.front: What is a bill of material on a drawing?
notes.back: A list of the materials and parts needed to fabricate or assemble a component or system.
notes.explanation: It is often included on the drawing, usually in ruled columns.
notes.example: Like the ingredients list above a recipe, but naming part numbers, quantities and where each part comes from.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Bill of Material”, p. 4-7
notes.evidence: A list of the materials and parts necessary for the fabrication or assembly of a component or system is often included on the drawing.

notes.front: What is a revision block on a drawing, and where is it usually found?
notes.back: Ruled columns listing changes to the drawing, usually beside the title block or at one corner of the drawing.
notes.explanation: Revisions come from changes in dimensions, design or materials; many firms also mark the title block to tell a revised drawing from its previous version.
introduces: revision block and current version of a drawing
notes.example: Like a document’s change history table, where each entry says what changed, when and on whose authority.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Revision Block”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: Revisions to a drawing are necessitated by changes in dimensions, design, or materials. The changes are usually listed in ruled columns either adjacent to the title block or at one corner of the drawing.
uses: revision block and current version of a drawing

notes.front: What are zone numbers on a drawing?
notes.back: Numbers and letters along the drawing’s borders, like those on a map, that help locate a point.
notes.explanation: They are used to find parts, sections and views on large drawings, particularly assembly drawings.
notes.example: Like the grid on a street atlas, where a street is found at row C, column 4.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Zone Numbers”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: Zone numbers on drawings are like the numbers and letters printed on the borders of a map. They help locate a point.

notes.front: What does a fuselage station number give?
notes.back: A location measured in inches from the aircraft’s reference point: fuselage station 185 is 185 inches from it.
notes.explanation: The measurement is usually taken from the nose or zero station, but some manufacturers use the firewall or another chosen point.
notes.example: Like the distance markers along a motorway, counted from one fixed starting point.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Station Numbers & Location Identification on Aircraft”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: A numbering system is used on large assemblies for aircraft to locate stations, such as fuselage frames. Fuselage station 185 indicates a location that is 185 inches from the datum of the aircraft.

notes.front: On a print, what is tolerance?
notes.back: The sum of the plus and minus allowance figures on a dimension.
notes.explanation: The plus figure is the maximum allowable variation and the minus figure the minimum, so their sum is the whole allowed spread.
notes.example: Like a speed limit band of 2 mph over and 3 mph under a target: the whole band is 5 mph wide.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Allowances & Tolerances”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: When a given dimension on a print shows an allowable variation, the plus (+) figure indicates the maximum, and the minus (−) figure the minimum allowable variation. The sum of the plus and minus allowance figures is called tolerance.

notes.front: What do finish marks on a drawing indicate?
notes.back: The surface that must be machine finished.
notes.explanation: Machine-finished surfaces look better and allow a closer fit with adjoining parts.
notes.example: Like a note on a table plan saying which edge must be planed smooth to butt against the wall.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Finish Marks”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: Finish marks are used to indicate the surface that must be machine finished. Such finished surfaces have a better appearance and allow a closer fit with adjoining parts.

notes.front: What does a drawing scale of 1:1 mean?
notes.back: The drawing is the same size as the part it shows.
notes.explanation: Other scales may be used, and computer drawings can easily be zoomed in or out.
notes.example: Like a life-size paper template of a gasket, rather than a half-size sketch of it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Scale”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: Some drawings are made the same size as the drawn part; reflecting a scale of 1:1. Other scales may be used.

notes.front: What is orthographic projection?
notes.back: The system of drawing several views of an object to show the exact size and shape of all its parts.
notes.explanation: Complex objects need several views to show exact size and shape, and orthographic projection supplies them.
notes.example: Like photographing a box straight on from the front, the top and one side, and laying the three pictures out together.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Orthographic Projection Drawings”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: To show the exact size and shape of all the parts of complex objects, several views are necessary. This is the system used in orthographic projection.

notes.front: What is a schematic diagram?
notes.back: A diagram that locates components with respect to each other within a system and shows its principle of operation.
notes.explanation: It does not show where components sit in the aircraft or their actual size and shape; it is often used for troubleshooting and training.
notes.example: Like a metro map: it shows how the stations connect, not where they really are in the city.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Schematic Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Schematic diagrams do not indicate the location of the individual components in the aircraft nor do they show the actual size and shape of the components, but rather locate components with respect to each other within the system.

notes.front: What is a flowchart used for?
notes.back: To illustrate a sequence or flow of events.
notes.explanation: The two types most used in aviation are troubleshooting flowcharts and logic flowcharts.
notes.example: Like a ‘does the kettle have power? yes/no’ chart taped inside a cupboard door.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Flowcharts”, p. 4-13
notes.evidence: Flowcharts are used to illustrate a sequence or flow of events.

notes.front: What does a centreline look like, and what does it show?
notes.back: Alternate long and short dashes; it indicates the centre of an object or of part of an object.
notes.explanation: Where centrelines cross, their short dashes intersect symmetrically.
notes.example: Like the dashed line painted down the middle of a road, but with long and short dashes alternating.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Centerlines”, p. 4-16
notes.evidence: Centerlines are made up of alternate long and short dashes. They indicate the center of an object or part of an object.

notes.front: What does a hidden line look like, and what does it show?
notes.back: Short, evenly spaced dashes; it shows edges or contours that cannot be seen.
notes.explanation: Hidden lines are frequently called dash lines.
notes.example: Like marking where a pipe runs behind a wall on a room plan, using dashes rather than a solid line.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Hidden Lines”, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: Hidden lines indicate invisible edges or contours. Hidden lines consist of short dashes evenly spaced and are frequently referred to as dash lines.

notes.front: What does a phantom line look like, and what does it show?
notes.back: One long and two short evenly spaced dashes; it shows an alternate position of part of the object, or where a missing part sits.
notes.explanation: Hidden lines, by contrast, are short dashes evenly spaced.
notes.example: Like a ghost outline showing where a door swings to when it is fully open.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Phantom Lines”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: Phantom lines indicate the alternate position of parts of the object or the relative position of a missing part. They are composed of one long and two short evenly spaced dashes.

notes.front: What does a cutting plane line indicate?
notes.back: The plane where a sectional view of the object is taken.
notes.explanation: A section labelled A-A, for example, is taken at the cutting plane line marked A.
notes.example: Like the knife mark on a loaf that shows where the slice in the photo was cut.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Cutting Plane and Viewing Plane Lines”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Cutting plane lines indicate the plane where a sectional view of the object is taken.

notes.front: What is a nomogram?
notes.back: A graph, usually of three sets of data, where knowing any two values gives the third.
notes.explanation: One type has three parallel scales, so a straight edge laid across two known values reads the third directly.
notes.example: Like a ready-reckoner where a ruler across speed and time shows distance on a third scale.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Nomograms”, p. 4-23
notes.evidence: A nomogram is a graph that usually consists of three sets of data. Knowledge of any two sets of data enables the interpreter to obtain the value for the third unknown corresponding value.

notes.front: What is microfiche?
notes.back: A card with pages laid out in a grid format.
notes.explanation: Like microfilm, it needs special devices both to read and to print the information.
notes.example: Like a contact sheet of photographs, where dozens of tiny pages share one card.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Microfilm & Microfiche”, p. 4-23
notes.evidence: Microfiche is a card with pages laid out in a grid format. Microfilm and microfiche require use of special devices for both reading and printing the information.

notes.front: Who may make notes or changes on a print, and what must they do?
notes.back: Only authorised individuals, and they must sign and date any change they make.
notes.explanation: Anyone else’s notes or marks may confuse others and lead to incorrect work.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Care & Use of Drawings”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: Never make notes or marks on a print, as they may confuse others and lead to incorrect work. Only authorized individuals are permitted to make notes or changes on prints, and they must sign and date any changes they make.

notes.front: Into which three classes may drawings be divided?
notes.back: Detail, assembly and installation.
notes.explanation: Each class answers a different question: one part, how parts relate, or where they sit in the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Types of Drawings”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: Drawings may be divided into three classes: detail, assembly, and installation.

notes.front: When is a full section view used?
notes.back: When the interior construction or hidden features of an object cannot be shown clearly by exterior views.
notes.explanation: Cutting the whole object open exposes its inside, such as the internal construction of a cable connector.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Full Section”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: A full section view is used when the interior construction or hidden features of an object cannot be shown clearly by exterior views.

notes.front: In a half section, how far does the cutting plane extend, and what is it used for?
notes.back: Only halfway across the object; it is used with symmetrical objects to show both interior and exterior.
notes.explanation: The uncut half stays as an exterior view, so one drawing shows the outside and the inside.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Half Section”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: In a half section, the cutting plane extends only halfway across the object, leaving the other half of the object as an exterior view. Half sections are used with symmetrical objects to show both the interior and exterior.

notes.front: Where is a revolved section drawn, and what does it show?
notes.back: Directly on the exterior view; it shows the shape of a part’s cross section, such as a wheel spoke.
notes.explanation: A removed section is drawn the same way but placed to one side.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Revolved Section”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: A revolved section drawn directly on the exterior view shows the shape of the cross section of a part, such as the spoke of a wheel.

notes.front: How does a removed section differ from a revolved section?
notes.back: It is placed at one side of the view, and often drawn to a larger scale to bring out details.
notes.explanation: Otherwise it is drawn like a revolved section.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Removed Section”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: A removed section illustrates parts of an object. It is drawn like revolved sections, except it is placed at one side and often drawn to a larger scale than the view indicated to bring out pertinent details.

notes.front: Where on a print is the title block usually found?
notes.back: In the lower right-hand corner; sometimes as a strip across almost the whole bottom of the sheet.
notes.explanation: Wherever it sits, it holds the drawing number and other data about the drawing and the object.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Title Blocks”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: This information is grouped in a prominent place on the print, usually in the lower right-hand corner. Sometimes the title block is in the form of a strip extending almost the entire distance across the bottom of the sheet.

notes.front: Besides the drawing number and the name of the part, what are two items of information a title block presents?
notes.back: Any two of: the drawing scale; the date; the name of the firm; the names of the draftsman, checker and approver.
notes.explanation: Title block layouts are not standard, but all present essentially these items.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Title Blocks”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: The drawing scale 4. The date 5. The name of the firm 6. The name of the draftsmen, the checker, and the person approving the drawing

notes.front: What is the drawing number in the title block for?
notes.back: To identify the print for filing and to prevent confusing it with any other print.
notes.explanation: It appears in a number block in the lower right corner of the title block, and may be repeated elsewhere so it shows when the print is folded or rolled.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Title Blocks”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: A drawing number to identify the print for filing purposes and to prevent confusing it with any other print.

notes.front: When left- and right-hand parts are mirror images, which is drawn and how is the other called for?
notes.back: The left-hand part is always shown; the right-hand part is called for in the title block by its dash number.
notes.explanation: Both parts carry the same number, and a note above the title block says which is shown and which is opposite.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reference and Dash Numbers”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: The lefthand part is always shown in the drawing. The right-hand part is called for in the title block.

notes.front: What are three items the columns of a bill of material provide?
notes.back: Any three of: part number; part name; material; quantity required; source of the part or material.
notes.explanation: The list covers the materials and parts needed to fabricate or assemble the item.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Bill of Material”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: provide the part number, name of the part, material the part is to be constructed of, the quantity required, and the source of the part or material.

notes.front: What are three items a revision block contains for each change?
notes.back: Any three of: identification symbol; date; nature of the revision; authority for the change; draftsman’s name.
notes.explanation: Together these show what changed, when, on whose authority and who drew the change.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Revision Block”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: The revision block contains the identification symbol, the date, the nature of the revision, the authority for the change, and the name of the draftsman who made the change.
uses: revision block and current version of a drawing

notes.front: Where must changes to approved drawings be noted?
notes.back: Carefully, on all existing prints of the drawing.
notes.explanation: Many firms also add a space in the title block for a symbol showing that the drawing has been revised.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Revision Block”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: All changes to approved drawings must be carefully noted on all existing prints of the drawing.
uses: revision block and current version of a drawing

notes.front: Which two drawing checks do the mechanic Airman Certification Standards list as risk-management elements for aircraft drawings?
notes.back: Applicability of the drawing to the particular aircraft by model and serial number, and identification of its current version.
notes.explanation: Both are listed under risk management in Task B, Aircraft Drawings.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation I, Task B (Aircraft Drawings), AM.I.B.R3 and R4, p. 8
notes.evidence: Applicability of the drawing or schematic to the particular aircraft by model and serial number. AM.I.B.R4 Identification of the current version and applicability of drawing being used.
uses: revision block and current version of a drawing

notes.front: Left-right locations and vertical locations on an aircraft are referenced to which lines?
notes.back: Left-right: the buttock line (butt stations). Vertical: the waterline.
notes.explanation: Together with fuselage stations fore and aft, these give a three-way address for any point.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Station Numbers & Location Identification on Aircraft”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: locations left and right of the aircraft’s longitudinal axis are made by reference to the buttock line and are called butt stations. Vertical locations on aircraft are made in reference to the waterline.

notes.front: When the plus and minus allowances are the same, they are written with a {{c1::±}} sign, and the tolerance is twice the allowance.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s 0.225 ± 0.0025 has a tolerance of 0.0050, the sum of the two equal allowances.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Allowances & Tolerances”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: If the plus and minus allowances are the same, you will find them presented as 0.225 ± 0.0025. The tolerance would then be 0.0050.

notes.front: When are decimal allowances used, and when are fractional allowances enough?
notes.back: Decimal when very accurate dimensions are needed; fractional when precise tolerances are not required.
notes.explanation: Allowance can be indicated in either fractional or decimal form.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Allowances & Tolerances”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: When very accurate dimensions are necessary, decimal allowances are used. Fractional allowances are sufficient when precise tolerances are not required.

notes.front: What is a print tolerance, and when does it apply?
notes.back: A general tolerance, usually in the title block, for noncritical dimensions; it applies wherever a dimension line shows no tolerance.
notes.explanation: It covers dimensions whose exact size is noncritical.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading and Interpreting Drawings”, p. 4-21
notes.evidence: A print tolerance (usually found in the title block) is a general tolerance that can be applied to parts where the dimensions are noncritical. Where a tolerance is not shown on a dimension line, the print tolerance applies.

notes.front: Does a finish mark call for paint, enamel or plating?
notes.back: No. A finish mark calls for a machined finish, not a coating.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns not to confuse machined finishes with paint, enamel, chromium plating and similar coatings; limits and tolerances still apply while finishing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Finish Marks”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: During the finishing process, the required limits and tolerances must be observed. Do not confuse machined finishes with those of paint, enamel, chromium plating, and similar coating.

notes.front: How many possible views does orthographic projection have, and why?
notes.back: Six, because all objects have six sides: front, top, bottom, rear, right side and left side.
notes.explanation: Picture the object in a transparent hinged box: each side of the box carries one view, and the box opens flat.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Orthographic Projection Drawings”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: In orthographic projection, there are six possible views of an object, because all objects have six sides—front, top, bottom, rear, right side, and left side.

notes.front: Which orthographic drawings are most common, and which view is the principal view?
notes.back: One-, two- and three-view drawings; the front view is the principal view.
notes.explanation: It is seldom necessary to show all six views, so only those needed are drawn.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Orthographic Projection Drawings”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: One-, two-, and three-view drawings are the most common. Regardless of the number of views used, the arrangement is generally as shown in Figure 4-11, with the front view as principal view.

notes.front: What is a detail view, and how is its area marked on the principal view?
notes.back: A view of part of the object in greater detail and to a larger scale; the area is usually encircled by a heavy line.
notes.explanation: Aircraft drawings seldom show more than two principal views, relying instead on detail or sectional views.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Detail View”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: A detail view shows only a part of the object, but in greater detail and to a larger scale than the principal view. The part that is shown in detail elsewhere on the drawing is usually encircled by a heavy line on the principal view.

notes.front: Why are angles and dimensions not accurate in a perspective drawing?
notes.back: Because of perspective, some lines of the object are not parallel.
notes.explanation: A perspective view shows the object as an observer sees it, most like a photograph.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Perspective Drawings”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Because of perspective, some of the lines of an object are not parallel and therefore the actual angles and dimensions are not accurate.

notes.front: How are lines drawn in an isometric drawing, compared with a perspective drawing?
notes.back: Parallel, and dimensioned as in an orthographic projection, whereas perspective lines converge.
notes.explanation: An isometric view tilts the object forward so portions of three views show at once.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Isometric Drawings”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Unlike a perspective drawing where lines converge and dimensions are not true, lines in an isometric drawing are parallel and dimensioned as they are in an orthographic projection.

notes.front: What one difference sets an oblique drawing apart from an isometric one?
notes.back: In an oblique drawing, two of the three drawing axes are always at right angles to each other.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the handbook describes an oblique view as like an isometric view.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Oblique Drawings”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: An oblique view is like an isometric view, except for one distinct difference. In an oblique drawing, two of the three drawing axes are always at right angles to each other.

notes.front: What does an exploded view drawing show, and where is it often used?
notes.back: The individual parts of an assembly and their relative positions before assembly; often in illustrated parts catalogues for ordering parts.
notes.explanation: Its numbers correspond to a list of part numbers.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Exploded View Drawings”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: The view shows the individual parts and their relative position to the other parts before they are assembled. [Figure 4-17] Exploded view drawings are often used in IPCs that are used to order parts.

notes.front: Into which four types may the diagrams an aviation mechanic uses be grouped?
notes.back: Installation, schematic, block and wiring diagrams.
notes.explanation: There are many types of diagrams, but these are the ones a mechanic meets on the job.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: those that the aviation mechanic is concerned with during the performance of their job may be grouped into four classes or types: installation, schematic, block, and wiring diagrams.

notes.front: What does an installation diagram show?
notes.back: Each component in the system and its location in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: That makes it invaluable for identifying and locating components; it is used widely in maintenance and repair manuals.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Installation Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: It identifies each of the components in the systems and shows their location in the aircraft.

notes.front: For what purposes are schematic diagrams often used?
notes.back: Troubleshooting and training.
notes.explanation: They show the principle of operation of an aircraft system rather than where parts are.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Schematic Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Schematics show the principle of operation of an aircraft system and are often used for troubleshooting and training purposes.

notes.front: How is each component drawn in a block diagram?
notes.back: As a rectangle (block), with lines connecting it to the other blocks it interfaces with.
notes.explanation: Block diagrams show a simplified relationship of a more complex system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Block Diagrams”, p. 4-13
notes.evidence: Individual components are drawn as a rectangle (block) with lines connecting it to other components (blocks) that it interfaces with during operation.

notes.front: What do wiring diagrams show?
notes.back: The electrical wiring and circuitry, coded for identification, of all the electrical appliances and devices on the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Even for simple circuits they can be quite complicated; for technicians doing electrical work, a thorough knowledge of them is essential.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Wiring Diagrams”, p. 4-13
notes.evidence: Wiring diagrams show the electrical wiring and circuitry, coded for identification, of all the electrical appliances and devices used on aircraft.

notes.front: How does a troubleshooting flowchart lead to a solution?
notes.back: Through a series of yes or no questions, each answer leading to a different course of action.
notes.explanation: In this simple manner a logical solution to a problem may be reached.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Troubleshooting Flowchart”, p. 4-15
notes.evidence: is yes, one course of action is followed. If the answer is no, a different course of action is followed. In this simple manner, a logical solution to a problem may be achieved.

notes.front: Most drawings use three widths, or intensities, of lines: {{c1::thin, medium and thick}}.
notes.explanation: Widths vary somewhat between drawings, but a thin and a thick line always look noticeably different.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Lines and Their Meanings”, p. 4-16
notes.evidence: Most drawings use three widths, or intensities, of lines: thin, medium, or thick.

notes.front: What does a dimension line look like?
notes.back: A light solid line, broken at the midpoint for the measurement, with opposite-pointing arrowheads at each end.
notes.explanation: The arrowheads show where the measurement starts and ends.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Dimension Lines”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: A dimension line is a light solid line, broken at the midpoint for insertion of measurement indications, and having opposite pointing arrowheads at each end to show origin and termination of a measurement.

notes.front: What is a leader line?
notes.back: A solid line with one arrowhead, pointing to the part a note, number or other reference applies to.
notes.explanation: It ties text on the drawing to the exact feature it describes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Leader Lines”, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: Leader lines are solid lines with one arrowhead. They indicate a part or portion that a note, number, or other reference applies.

notes.front: What does the outline or visible line represent, and how wide is it?
notes.back: Edges and surfaces seen when the object is viewed directly; a medium-to-wide line.
notes.explanation: It is used for all lines representing visible lines on the object.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Outline or Visible Lines”, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: The outline or visible line is used for all lines on the drawing representing visible lines on the object. This is a medium-towide line that represents edges and surfaces that can be seen when the object is viewed directly.

notes.front: What do stitch lines indicate, and how do their dashes compare with hidden lines?
notes.back: Stitching or sewing lines; very short dashes about half the length of hidden-line dashes.
notes.explanation: Long lines of stitching may be shown as stitch lines connected by phantom lines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Stitch Lines”, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: Stitch lines are used to indicate the stitching or sewing lines on an article and consists of a series of very short dashes, approximately half the length of dash or hidden lines, evenly spaced.

notes.front: What do material symbols (section line symbols) show?
notes.back: The kind of material the part is to be made from.
notes.explanation: If the exact specification appears elsewhere, the easier cast-iron symbol may be used and the material listed in the bill of material or a note.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Material Symbols”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Section line symbols show the kind of material from which the part is to be constructed.

notes.front: How are shape symbols usually shown on a drawing?
notes.back: As a revolved or removed section.
notes.explanation: They show the shape of an object, such as an angle, channel or tube, at a glance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Shape Symbols”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Shape symbols are usually shown on a drawing as a revolved or removed section.

notes.front: What do electrical symbols represent?
notes.back: Electrical devices, instead of an actual drawing of the units.
notes.explanation: Once the symbols are learned, an electrical diagram shows what each unit is, what it does and how it is connected.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Electrical Symbols”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Electrical symbols represent various electrical devices rather than an actual drawing of the units.

notes.front: On opening a drawing, what should be read and checked before reading the illustrations?
notes.back: The drawing number and description; then the model affected, the latest change letter and the next assembly listed.
notes.explanation: These checks confirm the drawing is the correct one before any work is based on it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading and Interpreting Drawings”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Upon opening a drawing, read the drawing number and the description of the article. Next, check the model affected, the latest change letter, and the next assembly listed.

notes.front: In a multiview drawing, why can one view not be read on its own?
notes.back: Each line shows a change in direction of a surface, but another view is needed to tell what the change is.
notes.explanation: A circle in one view could be a hole or a protruding boss; only the adjacent view settles it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading and Interpreting Drawings”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Each line on a view represents a change in the direction of a surface, but another view must be consulted to determine what the change is.

notes.front: If a dimension on a drawing has no inch mark, the dimension is in {{c1::inches}}.
notes.explanation: Dimensions may be written with or without the inch mark.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading and Interpreting Drawings”, p. 4-20
notes.evidence: Dimensions are indicated by figures either with or without the inch mark. If no inch mark is used, the dimension is in inches.

notes.front: What must a repair sketch provide, and how complete must it be?
notes.back: All necessary information for those making the repair or part; completeness depends on its intended use.
notes.explanation: A purely pictorial sketch needs no dimensions, but a part to be made from it needs all construction details.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Repair Sketches”, p. 4-22
notes.evidence: Such a sketch must provide all necessary information to those who must make the repair or manufacture the part. The degree that a sketch is complete depends on its intended use.

notes.front: When reading a graph or chart, what must be carefully understood first?
notes.back: All the notes and legend information.
notes.explanation: Doing so removes any misinterpretation of the information presented.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading & Interpreting Graphs & Charts”, p. 4-23
notes.evidence: When interpreting information shown on graphs and charts, it is extremely important that all the notes and legend information be carefully understood to eliminate any misinterpretation of the information presented.

notes.front: In the figure, which numbered line shows edges that cannot be seen from the viewing direction?
notes.back: D) Line 2
notes.choices:
A) Line 1
B) Line 4
C) Line 3
D) Line 2
notes.choicesExplained: A is a centreline, marking the centre of an object. C is a phantom line, showing an alternate or missing part’s position. B is a stitch line, marking sewing lines.
notes.explanation: Hidden lines, made of short evenly spaced dashes, show invisible edges or contours.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Hidden Lines”, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: Hidden lines indicate invisible edges or contours. Hidden lines consist of short dashes evenly spaced

image.alt: Five horizontal lines numbered 1 to 5. Line 1 alternates long and short dashes. Line 2 is short dashes evenly spaced. Line 3 repeats one long dash followed by two short dashes. Line 4 is very short dashes, about half the length of line 2's. Line 5 is a continuous thick solid line.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA-H-8083-30B, Chapter 4, “Lines and Their Meanings”

notes.front: A drawing of a control surface must show it both at rest and at full deflection in one view. Which line shows the deflected position?
notes.back: C) Phantom line
notes.choices:
A) Hidden line
B) Centreline
C) Phantom line
D) Cutting plane line
notes.choicesExplained: A shows invisible edges, not another position. B marks the centre of an object. D marks where a section is taken.
notes.explanation: Phantom lines show the alternate position of parts of an object.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Phantom Lines”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: Phantom lines indicate the alternate position of parts of the object or the relative position of a missing part.

notes.front: A technician needs the material, size and method of manufacture of one replacement spacer, and nothing else. Which drawing class gives exactly that?
notes.back: A) Detail drawing
notes.choices:
A) Detail drawing
B) Assembly drawing
C) Installation drawing
D) Schematic diagram
notes.choicesExplained: B shows how two or more parts relate. C shows a part or assembly in its installed position. D shows how a system’s components relate in operation.
notes.explanation: A detail drawing describes a single part with the specifications for making it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Types of Drawings”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: A detail drawing is a description of a single part, describing bylines, notes, and symbols the specifications for size, shape, material, and methods of manufacture

notes.front: A mechanic must fit a new bracket assembly and needs its position relative to nearby frames in the finished aircraft. Which drawing class answers this?
notes.back: C) Installation drawing
notes.choices:
A) Detail drawing
B) Assembly drawing
C) Installation drawing
D) Block diagram
notes.choicesExplained: A covers one part’s manufacture. B shows how the bracket’s own parts relate, not where it sits. D shows a simplified system relationship.
notes.explanation: An installation drawing gives a part or assembly in its final installed position, with locating dimensions.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Installation Drawing”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: It shows the dimensions necessary for the location of specific parts with relation to the other parts

notes.front: A drawing shows a pulley, its bushing, its bolt and its bracket together, mainly to show how they fit to one another. What class of drawing is it?
notes.back: D) Assembly drawing
notes.choices:
A) Detail drawing
B) Installation drawing
C) Wiring diagram
D) Assembly drawing
notes.choicesExplained: A would describe only one of those parts. B would locate the whole group in the aircraft. C shows electrical circuitry.
notes.explanation: An assembly drawing’s primary purpose is to show the relationship of its parts.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Assembly Drawing”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: Its primary purpose is to show the relationship of the various parts.

notes.front: A symmetrical valve body is drawn with one half cut away to show its passages and the other half left as an outside view. What kind of section is this?
notes.back: D) Half section
notes.choices:
A) Full section
B) Revolved section
C) Removed section
D) Half section
notes.choicesExplained: A cuts across the whole object. B is drawn on the exterior view to show a cross section. C is placed at one side, often at a larger scale.
notes.explanation: In a half section the cutting plane goes only halfway, so interior and exterior show together.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Half Section”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: In a half section, the cutting plane extends only halfway across the object, leaving the other half of the object as an exterior view.

notes.front: A print gives a bore as 1.250 +0.004 −0.001 inch. What are the largest and smallest acceptable sizes, and the tolerance?
notes.back: Largest 1.254; smallest 1.249; tolerance 0.005 inch.
notes.explanation: The plus figure sets the maximum and the minus figure the minimum, and tolerance is their sum.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Allowances & Tolerances”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: the plus (+) figure indicates the maximum, and the minus (−) figure the minimum allowable variation. The sum of the plus and minus allowance figures is called tolerance.

notes.front: A pin is dimensioned 0.500 ± 0.003 inch. A measured pin is 0.504 inch. Is it acceptable?
notes.back: A) No, it is 0.001 over the maximum of 0.503
notes.choices:
A) No, it is 0.001 over the maximum of 0.503
B) Yes, any size within 0.005 is acceptable
C) Yes, it is within the 0.006 tolerance
D) No, pins must be exactly 0.500
notes.choicesExplained: C confuses the total tolerance with the allowance on one side. B invents a limit not on the print. D ignores that the print allows variation.
notes.explanation: With equal allowances, 0.003 is allowed each way, so the maximum is 0.503.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Allowances & Tolerances”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: If the plus and minus allowances are the same, you will find them presented as 0.225 ± 0.0025.

notes.front: A noncritical dimension on a bracket drawing has no tolerance on its dimension line. What governs how far it may vary?
notes.back: C) The print tolerance, usually in the title block
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: it must be exact
B) The tolerance of the nearest dimension
C) The print tolerance, usually in the title block
D) The finish marks
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the general tolerance the print supplies. B borrows a tolerance meant for another feature. D show which surfaces are machine finished, not size limits.
notes.explanation: Where a dimension line shows no tolerance, the print tolerance applies.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading and Interpreting Drawings”, p. 4-21
notes.evidence: Where a tolerance is not shown on a dimension line, the print tolerance applies.

notes.front: A drawing shows part 51820-1 and notes “51820-2 opposite”. Which part is drawn, and what is 51820-2?
notes.back: 51820-1 is the drawn (left-hand) part; 51820-2 is the mirror-image opposite-hand part.
notes.explanation: The left-hand part is always shown, and the right-hand part is called for by its dash number.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reference and Dash Numbers”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: Both parts carry the same number, but the part called for is distinguished by a dash number.

notes.front: A technician notices what looks like a wrong hole size on a shop print. What should they do?
notes.back: C) Leave the print unmarked and refer it to someone authorised to change it
notes.choices:
A) Correct it on the print in pencil
B) Correct it and initial it
C) Leave the print unmarked and refer it to someone authorised to change it
D) Ignore it and drill to the print
notes.choicesExplained: A and B put an unauthorised mark on the print, which may confuse others. D risks incorrect work from a suspected error.
notes.explanation: Only authorised individuals may change prints, and they sign and date the change.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Care & Use of Drawings”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: Only authorized individuals are permitted to make notes or changes on prints, and they must sign and date any changes they make.

notes.front: Two prints of the same drawing number disagree on a rivet pitch. Where should the technician look first to tell which is current?
notes.back: D) The revision block of each print
notes.choices:
A) The drawing scale
B) The zone numbers
C) The bill of material
D) The revision block of each print
notes.choicesExplained: B) Zone numbers locate points on the sheet. C) The bill of material lists parts and materials. A) The scale gives the size ratio. None of them records changes.
notes.explanation: The revision block records each change with its symbol, date, nature and authority.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Revision Block”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: The revision block contains the identification symbol, the date, the nature of the revision, the authority for the change
uses: revision block and current version of a drawing

notes.front: A repair drawing for the right model is noted “serials 1005 thru 1336”. The aircraft in the hangar is serial 1402. What is the risk-managed response?
notes.back: B) Do not rely on it; find the drawing applicable to serial 1402
notes.choices:
A) Use it, since the model matches
B) Do not rely on it; find the drawing applicable to serial 1402
C) Use it, but add a note to the print
D) Scale the dimensions from a later print
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores serial-number applicability. C also puts an unauthorised note on a print. D measures from a print instead of using its dimensions.
notes.explanation: The mechanic certification standards ask applicants to manage the applicability of a drawing by model and serial number.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation I, Task B (Aircraft Drawings), AM.I.B.R3, p. 8
notes.evidence: Applicability of the drawing or schematic to the particular aircraft by model and serial number.

notes.front: A crack is reported at fuselage station 212 on an aircraft whose stations are measured from the nose. Where is it?
notes.back: 212 inches aft of the nose (zero station) along the fuselage.
notes.explanation: A fuselage station number is the distance in inches from the reference point, usually the nose.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Station Numbers & Location Identification on Aircraft”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: The measurement is usually taken from the nose or zero station, but in some instances, it may be taken from the firewall or some other point chosen by the manufacturer.

notes.front: An antenna must be mounted at a given height on the fin. Its vertical position will be given in reference to which line?
notes.back: A) Waterline
notes.choices:
A) Waterline
B) Buttock line
C) Fuselage station
D) Centreline of the wing
notes.choicesExplained: B gives left-right positions. C gives fore-and-aft positions. D is wrong: wing stations are measured from the aircraft’s centreline, not the wing’s, and give spanwise positions, not heights.
notes.explanation: Vertical locations on aircraft are referenced to the waterline.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Station Numbers & Location Identification on Aircraft”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: Vertical locations on aircraft are made in reference to the waterline.

notes.front: Before building an assembly, a technician wants to order everything it needs. Which part of the drawing gives the quantities and sources?
notes.back: The bill of material.
notes.explanation: It lists part numbers, names, materials, quantities required and sources.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Bill of Material”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: provide the part number, name of the part, material the part is to be constructed of, the quantity required, and the source of the part or material.

notes.front: A trainee wants to understand how an air-conditioning system works in principle, not where its parts are. Which diagram suits best?
notes.back: D) Schematic diagram
notes.choices:
A) Installation diagram
B) Wiring diagram
C) Exploded view
D) Schematic diagram
notes.choicesExplained: A shows where components are located. B shows electrical wiring and circuitry. C shows parts before assembly, for ordering or assembly.
notes.explanation: Schematics show a system’s principle of operation and are used for training.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Schematic Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Schematics show the principle of operation of an aircraft system and are often used for troubleshooting and training purposes.

notes.front: A mechanic must find where a flight guidance computer is mounted in the flight deck. Which diagram is most useful?
notes.back: A) Installation diagram
notes.choices:
A) Installation diagram
B) Schematic diagram
C) Block diagram
D) Logic flowchart
notes.choicesExplained: B does not show component locations in the aircraft. C shows a simplified relationship of blocks. D analyses digital logic.
notes.explanation: Installation diagrams identify components and show their location in the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Installation Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Installation diagrams are used extensively in aircraft maintenance and repair manuals, and are invaluable in identifying and locating components

notes.front: A pictorial drawing shows three faces of a block at once, with all its edges drawn parallel and to true dimension. What type is it?
notes.back: C) Isometric
notes.choices:
A) Perspective
B) Exploded view
C) Isometric
D) Detail view
notes.choicesExplained: A has converging lines and inaccurate dimensions. B separates the parts of an assembly. D enlarges part of an orthographic view.
notes.explanation: Isometric lines are parallel and dimensioned as in orthographic projection.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Isometric Drawings”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: lines in an isometric drawing are parallel and dimensioned as they are in an orthographic projection.

notes.front: A top view shows two concentric circles on a casting. How does the reader tell whether each is a hole or a raised boss?
notes.back: By consulting the adjacent view, which shows the change in surface each circle represents.
notes.explanation: Where three views are given, all three must be consulted to be sure of the shape.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Reading and Interpreting Drawings”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: For example, a circle on one view may mean either a hole or a protruding boss

notes.front: A performance chart plots one value on the x axis and another on the y axis. How is a result usually read from it?
notes.back: Project up from the known x value and across from the known y value to the point that gives the result.
notes.explanation: Reading the notes and legend first avoids misreading the chart.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Graphs & Charts”, p. 4-23
notes.evidence: They often utilize values shown on the “x” and “y” axes that can be projected up and across to arrive at a specific result.

notes.front: A technician must draw a flat shim of uniform thickness. How many orthographic views are commonly enough, and how is thickness shown?
notes.back: One view, with a dimensional note giving the thickness.
notes.explanation: Only the views needed to show the object’s characteristics are drawn, and one view suffices for gaskets, shims and plates.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Orthographic Projection Drawings”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: uniform thickness, such as gaskets, shims, and plates. A dimensional note gives the thickness as shown in Figure 4-12.

notes.front: In a sectional view, two adjoining parts are filled with different section line patterns. What do the patterns tell the reader?
notes.back: C) The kind of material each part is made from
notes.choices:
A) Which surfaces are machine finished
B) Where the cutting plane lies
C) The kind of material each part is made from
D) Which part is hidden
notes.choicesExplained: A is shown by finish marks. B is shown by the cutting plane line. D is shown by hidden lines.
notes.explanation: Section line symbols are material symbols.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Material Symbols”, p. 4-19
notes.evidence: Section line symbols show the kind of material from which the part is to be constructed.

notes.front: How does a schematic diagram differ from an installation diagram?
notes.back: A schematic places components relative to each other in the system; an installation diagram shows where they are in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: A schematic shows neither location nor actual size and shape.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 4, Aircraft Drawings, “Schematic Diagrams”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: Schematic diagrams do not indicate the location of the individual components in the aircraft nor do they show the actual size and shape of the components
